cards.back: ΔH < 0 — heat released, products lower in energy than reactants. Container feels warm.
ΔH > 0 — heat absorbed, products higher in energy. Container feels cold (e.g. dissolving some salts).
Minimum energy colliding particles need to react — the peak minus reactants on an energy profile. Catalysts lower it; ΔH is unchanged.
Heat absorbed = mass of SOLUTION × specific heat capacity × temperature change. c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. m ≈ total solution volume in g.
ΔH is independent of route — enthalpy is a state function. Lets you calculate impossible-to-measure ΔH values from energy cycles.
Energy to break one mole of a specific bond in the GASEOUS state. Averaged across molecules — so calculated ΔH values differ slightly from experiment.
ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed. (Breaking absorbs, forming releases.)
ΔH making 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states (100 kPa, 298 K). Elements in standard states ≡ 0.
Dispersal of energy/particles: gas > liquid > solid; increases when gas moles increase. Units J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Spontaneous when ΔG < 0; ΔG = 0 at equilibrium. Convert ΔS to kJ before mixing units.
Yes, at ALL temperatures: both terms drive ΔG negative. (The other three sign combinations are temperature-dependent.)
Only above T = ΔH/ΔS (entropy-driven — e.g. melting ice above 0 °C).

cards.front: What does a catalyst NOT change?
cards.back: ΔH, ΔG or the equilibrium position — only Eᴀ and therefore rate. Thermodynamics vs kinetics distinction.

cards.front: Temperature fell during a reaction — sign of ΔH?
cards.back: Positive (endothermic): the mixture absorbed heat from its surroundings. Read the sign from the thermometer's direction.
≈ −54 to −57 kJ/mol for strong acid + strong base (per mole of water formed). Negative, because temperature RISES.

cards.front: Calorimetry trap: which mass goes into q = mcΔT?
cards.back: The whole solution heated (both volumes ≈ mass), not just the solute. Also divide by moles of WATER formed for neutralisation ΔH.

cards.front: Why are calculated bond-enthalpy ΔH values not exact?
cards.back: Average bond enthalpies ignore the molecule's specific environment — real bonds vary slightly. Experiment beats calculation.
Give an expected result WITH justification (Le Châtelier, ΔG cases). A bare answer loses the reasoning marks.

cards.front: Energy profile — what does a catalyst change on the diagram?
cards.back: Only the peak (Eᴀ) drops, via a new pathway. Reactant and product levels (ΔH) stay exactly the same.
